chunks.section: Representations have Trajectories: Characterizing Temporal Representation Dynamics in Neural Networks
chunks.text: Shivaprasad B. Gowda Affiliation: Indian Institute of Information Technology, Nagpur Email: bt24csa005@iiitn.ac.in Sparsh Mittal Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee Email: sparsh.mittal@mfs.iitr.ac.in

Recent work has shown that deep neural networks exhibit an implicit low-rank simplicity bias. In this paper, we investigate the questions that naturally arise from this observation. What are the temporal consequences of low-rank simplicity bias during optimization? How does representation geometry evolve throughout optimization rather than only at convergence? Do different neural architectures exhibit distinct geometric optimization behaviors? To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale empirical study tracking representational geometry throughout training. We find that neural networks follow three recurring geometric trajectories: persistent high-rank, collapse-and-recovery, and persistent low-rank. We further identify Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC) as a pathological regime in which representations collapse to rank-one and fail to recover, leading to a sustained loss of representational capacity. While collapse-and-recovery is consistently associated with successful optimization in controlled settings, experiments on real-world models show that the relationship between geometric trajectories and optimization outcomes is configuration dependent. Overall, our findings suggest that representation geometry evolves dynamically during training and provide a new perspective on how deep neural networks learn.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) learn task-relevant representations through nonlinear transformations that evolve throughout optimization ( Bengio et al., 2013 ; Saxe et al., 2014 ; Baratin et al., 2021 ) . This evolution, termed representation dynamics , offers insight into how networks learn beyond their final representations. Prior work shows that DNNs exhibit an implicit low-rank bias ( Huh et al., 2023 ) , and that under suitable conditions, finite-depth networks can recover the target function’s rank ( Jacot, 2023 ) . However, existing studies largely characterize representations at convergence, leaving their evolution during optimization less understood. We therefore ask: How does representation geometry evolve during optimization, do architectures exhibit distinct trajectories, and are these trajectories associated with optimization success or failure? Contributions. We investigate these questions and make the following observations. In controlled settings, runs can be partitioned into recurring geometric trajectory archetypes. These trajectories include persistent high-rank behavior, transient representation collapse followed by recovery, and persistent low-rank behavior. The prevalence of these trajectories varies considerably across different architectures, optimization settings, and activation functions. To characterize the pathological extreme of persistent low-rank behavior, we introduce Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC): a persistent rank-one state that, in our experiments, is already present at the first logged epoch and is not escaped during training. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 1. A large-scale empirical study of temporal representation geometry during optimization.

2. Identification and characterization of three recurring rank trajectories. 3. Introduction of DRC, with evidence that it is present early, grows with depth, and is rarer with residual connections. 4. Statistical evidence that trajectory types are associated with optimization outcomes at convergence. 5. Evidence that trajectory category at early training milestones forecasts eventual optimization success, replicated across synthetic MLPs. 6. CIFAR-10 experiments across MLP, CNN, ResNet, and ViT architectures, replicating the synthetic taxonomy across four architecture families.

Implicit Low-Rank Bias: Gunasekar et al. (2017) showed that gradient descent in matrix factorization implicitly favors low nuclear-norm solutions, while Arora et al. (2019) showed that depth strengthens this low-rank bias. Huh et al. (2023) found that DNNs favor lower-rank representations and can exploit this bias without increasing capacity. Razin and Cohen (2020) showed that implicit regularization in deep matrix factorization cannot be reduced to simple norm minimization, and Jacot (2023) showed that finite-depth networks can recover the target function’s bottleneck rank. These works focus primarily on low-rank solutions or the final rank rather than its evolution during training. Representation Geometry: Papyan et al. (2020) showed that deep networks develop structured representations through Neural Collapse, while Baratin et al. (2021) linked implicit regularization to dynamic alignment with task-relevant directions. Súkeník et al. (2024) showed that regularized low-rank solutions can achieve lower loss than DNC, while Garrod and Keating (2026) found that DNC persists under cross-entropy as a stable critical point with a larger optimization basin. Saxe et al. (2014) showed that deep linear networks follow nonlinear learning trajectories with long plateaus and rapid convergence. Unlike Dohare et al. (2024) , which studies continual learning degradation, we examine temporal representation dynamics and characterize DRC, a persistent rank-one state associated with optimization failure.

Existing work links DNN implicit bias to low-rank representations, neural collapse, and structured feature geometry, but largely studies final representations or optimization behavior rather than temporal evolution of representation. We address this gap through a layer-wise study of 4,084 4{,}084 controlled synthetic runs, identifying trajectory archetypes missed by endpoint analyses. Representation collapse has also been studied in self-supervised learning ( Jing et al., 2022 ) , GNN over-smoothing ( Li et al., 2018 ; Oono and Suzuki, 2020 ) , and Transformer attention collapse ( Dong et al., 2021 ) . Unlike these settings, we study DRC as a persistent rank bottleneck during supervised training associated with optimization failure. Rank contraction in supervised networks has likewise been linked to depth: Daneshmand et al. (2020) found stable-rank collapse at initialization in unnormalized networks, prevented by batch normalization, while Feng et al. (2022) observed decreasing feature and Jacobian rank across layers. Signal-propagation analyses ( Poole et al., 2016 ; Schoenholz et al., 2017 ; Pennington et al., 2017 ) describe ordered and chaotic regimes through the evolution of input correlations; our DRC regime is closely related to the ordered phase, appearing from the first logged epoch and becoming more prevalent with depth. Complementarily, we track full training trajectories, distinguishing runs that escape low-rank states from those that exhibit persistent collapse, and relate these trajectories to optimization outcomes across architectures and optimizers. Although effective rank has been used to assess representation quality and downstream performance ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) , we use it as a training-time criterion for identifying collapse.

Stable Rank. ( Rudelson and Vershynin, 2007 ) measures how dominant the single strongest direction is relative to the total spectral energy. It is the ratio of the squared Frobenius norm to the squared spectral norm of the activation matrix: srank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ( ℓ ) ) = ‖ 𝐇 ( ℓ ) ‖ F 2 ‖ 𝐇 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 2 \mathrm{srank}(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)})=\frac{\|\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}^{2}} Effective Rank. ( Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ) measures how many directions carry meaningful mass across the entire spectrum via entropy, capturing representational diversity that becomes hard for stable rank to capture once the tail is small relative to σ 1 \sigma_{1} . Computed as the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the normalized singular values of the activation matrix: erank ( 𝐇 ( ℓ ) ) = exp ( − ∑ i p i ln p i ) \mathrm{erank}(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)})=\exp\!\left(-\sum_{i}p_{i}\ln p_{i}\right) , where p i = σ i ∑ j σ j p_{i}=\frac{\sigma_{i}}{\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}} . Stable rank is anchored to spectral norm, so it is particularly sensitive to the dominance of a single leading direction, but is comparatively insensitive to how mass is distributed across the remaining spectrum once that mass is small relative to σ 1 \sigma_{1} . Effective rank is sensitive to how many directions carry non-trivial mass in aggregate, but is less sensitive to extreme dominance by a single direction as long as some distributed tail persists.

Tracking representation geometry throughout optimization shows that runs can be partitioned into recurring geometric trajectory archetypes according to the operational criteria in Table 1 . These trajectories differ in how the representation geometry evolves over the course of optimization. Figure 1 visualizes examples. Figure 1: Archetypal representation geometry trajectories: (a) persistent high rank, (b) collapse-and-recovery, and (c) persistent low rank. The x-axis uses a symlog scale to resolve early dynamics. Archetype 1 (A1): Persistent High Rank. Throughout optimization, both stable and effective rank remain consistently high with minor fluctuations, indicating that representations preserve their high-dimensional geometry throughout training. Archetype 2 (A2): Collapse and Recovery. A2 runs are those in which the stable rank reaches or drops below the collapse threshold of 1.5 1.5 at some logged epoch and later rises above it by more than 0.1 0.1 . In the example shown in Figure 1 (b), this recovery is accompanied by a clear drop in loss. A2 behavior occurs under both default and low-rank initialization (Table S.5 ). Archetype 3 (A3): Persistent Low Rank. Representations enter a low-rank regime early in optimization and remain there for the rest of training. Unlike Archetype 2, little or no recovery in representational rank is observed afterward.

DRC: Destructive Representation Collapse. Within the persistent low-rank regime, we identify an extreme case in which representations are effectively one-dimensional and remain so. Because stable rank alone cannot distinguish moderately low-rank representations from complete collapse, DRC is defined jointly using stable and effective rank (Eq. 1 ). In our experiments, most DRC runs are already at SR ≤ 1.05 \leq 1.05 at the first logged epoch (Section 7 ), so DRC is better understood as a failure to escape an early rank-one state than as a collapse that develops later in training. We next examine whether the discovered trajectory archetypes are associated with optimization outcomes. Across all convergence thresholds, Collapse-and-Recovery (A2) trajectories consistently show the highest success rates, whereas DRC exhibits the lowest. At the strict 10 − 3 10^{-3} threshold, optimization success reaches 82.89 % 82.89\% for A2 but only 0.90 % 0.90\% for DRC; A1 and A3 lie between these extremes at 35.11 % 35.11\% and 40.96 % 40.96\% , respectively. At this threshold, recovery trajectories are 3.07 × 3.07\times more likely to optimize successfully than non-recovery trajectories. We tested this association using Fisher’s exact test ( Fisher, 1922 ) and examined whether it persists after controlling for architectural and optimization factors. Archetypes are defined from the trajectory, including its final epoch, so these are associations rather than prospective effects (Table 2 ). Early trajectory forecasting and association with outcomes. Trajectory category provides a strong early signal of eventual optimization success in synthetic MLPs. Using only information available at each milestone, without final-epoch leakage, trajectory categories at 10 % , 25 % 10\%,25\% , and 50 % 50\% of training predict eventual success with odds ratios of 6.33 × 6.33\times , 10.60 × 10.60\times , and 12.11 × 12.11\times , respectively. The classification uses only information available up to the respective milestone and does not use final loss or final representations. These effects remain stable across 20 threshold combinations (Appendix Sec. E , F ). The 25 % 25\% milestone therefore provides a particularly clear early indication of eventual optimization success. For completeness, retrospective association analyses using the full trajectory show that adding trajectory archetypes to hyperparameter controls increases AUC from 0.9459 0.9459 to 0.9660 0.9660 (accuracy 90.77 % → 92.58 % 90.77\%\rightarrow 92.58\% ), while final-rank metrics alone achieve an AUC of 0.7743 0.7743 ( 69.20 % 69.20\% ) (Table S.9 ).

Figure 3: Empirical separation of DRC from moderate low-rank collapse (A3). Prior work has shown that deep networks develop low-rank representations and that rank contracts with depth in unnormalized feedforward networks (Sec. 2 ). In our synthetic experiments, the most severe form of this contraction, an effectively rank-one representation, becomes more frequent with depth in networks without residual connections or depth-dependent scaling (Fig. S.4 ), varies with activation function (Fig. S.5 ), and is associated with optimization failure (Figs 3 - 4 , Tables S.3 - S.4 ). We call this state DRC. Stable rank alone does not identify complete collapse; it is dominated by the leading singular value σ 1 \sigma_{1} and is insensitive to the rest of the spectrum. A model can have low stable rank (SR ≈ 1.05 ​ – ​ 1.19 \approx 1.05–1.19 ) while retaining substantial effective rank (ER ≥ 10.4 \geq 10.4 ), as in a Plain CNN run that reaches 90.35 % 90.35\% CIFAR-10 test accuracy (Table S.7 , Fig. S.6 ). Each component captures a different aspect of collapse. The minimum stable rank indicates whether the representation ever collapses to a nearly one-dimensional state; the final stable rank confirms that it never recovers, and the effective-rank criterion ensures that the remaining singular-value spectrum has also collapsed rather than retaining meaningful high-dimensional structure. Appendix Sec. C justifies the selected thresholds to define DRC. Across the synthetic pool, DRC occurs in 1,106 1,106 of 4,084 4,084 runs ( 27.08 % ) (27.08\%) , but its prevalence varies substantially by architecture: 60.32 % 60.32\% of Deep Linear runs, 43.62 % 43.62\% of Plain MLP runs, and 8.51 % 8.51\% of Residual MLP runs exhibit DRC. Architecture-wise breakdown is reported in Table S.4 . Two observations support the association of DRC with optimization failure. 1. For image classification on CIFAR-10, all 100.0 % 100.0\% of models ( 41 / 41 ) (41/41) that entered the DRC regime collapse to a random guess (Accuracy ≤ 10.15 % \leq 10.15\% , mean 9.99 % 9.99\% ), with cross-entropy loss freezing at baseline ≈ 2.3026 \approx 2.3026 .

2. In synthetic matrix regression, DRC accounts for 1,106 1{,}106 of 4,084 4{,}084 synthetic runs ( 27.08 % 27.08\% ). Crucially, 100.0 % 100.0\% of all numerical loss explosions ( 152 / 152 152/152 runs with ℒ > 100 \mathcal{L}>100 ) occur exclusively within the DRC regime, with losses expanding up to 10 15 10^{15} . Exploding activations are themselves dominated by a single direction, so these runs are not independent evidence that collapse precedes failure. Among the 954 954 non-divergent DRC runs, the vast majority fail to optimize, freezing at high unlearned baseline loss ( median MSE ≈ 0.29 \text{median MSE}\approx 0.29 ), while only 0.90 % 0.90\% of all DRC runs reach L < 10 − 3 L<10^{-3} (Table S.3 ) Figure 4: Layer-wise stable rank dynamics: deeper layers undergo DRC without recovery. When DRC arises. In the three-seed grid ( 6,804 CLOSE (6,804 runs), all 2,846 2,846 models already have SR ≤ 1.05 \leq 1.05 at epoch 1. With full-batch training, epoch 1 is one gradient step from initialization, indicating that DRC is present essentially from the start rather than emerging during training, consistent with signal-propagation failure in deep unnormalized networks (Sec. 2 ). DRC is less prevalent with default initialization ( 29.3 % 29.3\% ) than with the rank-one initialization ( 54.4 % 54.4\% ) used in half the grid (Table S.5 ), but remains frequent under default initialization. We therefore interpret DRC as identifying runs trapped in an early rank-one state, not as evidence that training dynamics cause rank collapse. The probability that a model undergoes DRC scales nearly monotonically with architectural depth L L . (Fig. S.4 ).

Importantly, our results show that low-rank representations should not be viewed as uniformly pathological. Instead, DRC represents an extreme point on the low-rank spectrum that is consistently associated with optimization failure (Fig. 3 ).

The preceding sections establish the proposed trajectory taxonomy using controlled matrix regression experiments. To test consistency, we now ask which of these patterns appear in 306 306 CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) vision models, spanning MLP, CNN, ViTs and residual architectures.

Across broader CIFAR-10 architectural sweeps, representational trajectories exhibit the following patterns: Plain MLPs. As in the controlled experiments, models following the recovery trajectory consistently optimize better than those remaining in the persistent low-rank regime. Recovery is associated with lower training loss ( 0.8380 0.8380 A2 vs. 2.0072 2.0072 A3; 1.1692 1.1692 nats reduction) and test loss ( 1.5204 1.5204 A2 vs. 2.1899 2.1899 A3) (Table S.26 ). This is consistent with the synthetic results. Residual MLPs and ResNets. In the CIFAR-10 sweeps, residual architectures reached low training and test loss and did not enter the DRC regime. The 6 6 ResNet runs (ResNet − 18 / 50 × 3 -18/50\times 3 skip modes) retain high effective rank ( 11.58 ​ – ​ 14.45 ) (11.58–14.45) at the end of training. These observations are consistent with skip connections delaying rank decay (Section 6 ). Vision Transformers. Across 48 CIFAR-10 ViT runs with and without residual connections, no-residual ViTs showed strong depth-wise rank contraction, with 2 of the 8 depth-9 no-residual runs collapsing under the dual-metric DRC criterion to rank one at chance accuracy, whereas zero residual ViTs collapsed (Table S.10 ). Early Recovery runs showed substantially higher eventual success than Early Stuck runs, with odds ratios of 23.00 × 23.00\times , 12.78 × 12.78\times , and 12.78 × 12.78\times at 10 % , 25 % , 10\%,25\%, and 50 % 50\% of training, respectively (Table S.12 ), indicating the geometric framework extends to Vision Transformers; full details are in Appendix Sec. chunks.section: 8.2 Dead gradient effect in Plain Deep CNNs.
chunks.text: In plain feedforward CNNs ( M models = 192 M_{\mathrm{models}}=192 ), a superficial examination suggests an apparent contradiction: models achieving low cross-entropy loss predominantly reside in the low-rank regime ( SR final ≤ 1.5 \text{SR}_{\text{final}}\leq 1.5 ), whereas high-rank networks exhibit poor loss optimization. Tracking layerwise gradient norms ( ‖ g l ‖ \|g_{l}\| ) resolves this issue: 1. Dead-Gradient High-Rank scenario : 9.38 % 9.38\% of plain CNN runs ( 18 / 192 18/192 ) remain in Archetype 1. Crucially, 100.0 % 100.0\% of these 18 high-rank models failed to optimize, freezing at high test cross-entropy loss ( mean = 2.6445 \text{mean}=2.6445 , range: 2.3353 − 2.7659 2.3353-2.7659 ) and high training loss ( mean = 2.6550 \text{mean}=2.6550 ). chunks.section: 8.2 Dead gradient effect in Plain Deep CNNs.
chunks.text: These findings align with Section 7 : low-rank representations are not inherently pathological, but the rank-one DRC regime and high-rank runs with vanished gradients are both associated with failure. Rank metrics, therefore, complement rather than replace loss curves and gradient diagnostics. Since DRC is visible at the first logged epoch, monitoring SR and ER could help flag doomed runs early, although we have not tested this as an early-stopping rule.

Overall, representation trajectories reveal optimization behavior beyond static endpoints: successful runs tend to avoid persistent Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC), while recovery from low-rank states is associated with convergence. Residual connections are associated with fewer DRC cases and delayed rank decay, and trajectory categories at 25 % 25\% of training already forecast eventual outcomes, suggesting potential prospective value. Future work includes formal bounds, comparisons with Hessian, edge-of-stability, and plasticity-loss diagnostics (e.g., dormant neurons), activation-centering and stabilization in ViTs, larger per-architecture CIFAR-10 sweeps, higher-order spectral measures such as Schatten norms and singular-value decay, and evaluating early-milestone trajectory categories as practical early-stopping signals.

chunks.section: Appendix E Early-Trajectory Prediction of Optimization Outcomes
chunks.text: To examine whether representation dynamics contain information about optimization outcomes before convergence, we classified models using trajectory information available at early training milestones of 10 % 10\% , 25 % 25\% , and 50 % 50\% of training. For synthetic MLPs, these correspond to epochs 100, 250, and 500 of a 1,000-epoch run. Models were assigned to an early trajectory category based on the minimum stable rank observed up to each milestone and its subsequent change: Never Collapsed if S ​ R t > 1.50 SR_{t}>1.50 throughout the observed interval, Early Recovery if the representation had collapsed but subsequently expanded, and Early Stuck if it remained near the collapse bottleneck. The classification uses only information available up to the respective milestone and does not use final loss or final representations. Across 2,268 2,268 synthetic MLP runs, the early trajectory categories differ in their eventual optimization outcomes. At 25 % 25\% of training, 618 models were classified as Early Recovery, with a 35.8 % 35.8\% success rate, compared with 4.9 % 4.9\% among the 930 930 Early Stuck models. This corresponds to a relative risk of 7.16 × 7.16\times and an odds ratio of 10.60 10.60 . Similar differences are observed at 10 % 10\% and 50 % 50\% , with odds ratios of 6.33 6.33 and 12.11 12.11 , respectively. These comparisons are unadjusted for configuration (activation, optimizer, depth, initialization) and should be read as descriptive.

chunks.section: Appendix E Early-Trajectory Prediction of Optimization Outcomes
chunks.text: Overall, these results suggest that representation trajectories contain information that is related to eventual optimization outcomes before convergence. In particular, models that remain near the rank-collapse bottleneck early in training tend to have lower subsequent success rates, whereas models showing early recovery tend to have better outcomes. This result is consistent with early trajectory carrying forecasting information, we do not yet test whether it can be turned into a reliable automated early-stopping criterion, which we leave to future work.

chunks.section: Appendix F Sensitivity to Trajectory Classification Thresholds
chunks.text: This is a robustness check of the early-milestone forecasting result in Appendix E . To examine how sensitive the trajectory–outcome relationship is to the chosen numerical boundaries, we repeated the archetype classification at the 25 % 25\% training milestone ( e ​ p ​ o ​ c ​ h ​ 250 ) (epoch250) across a grid of collapse and recovery thresholds. The collapse threshold τ collapse \tau_{\mathrm{collapse}} was varied over { 1.05 , 1.10 , 1.15 , 1.20 , 1.50 } \{1.05,1.10,1.15,1.20,1.50\} , and the recovery threshold Δ ​ τ rec \Delta\tau_{\mathrm{rec}} over { 0.05 , 0.10 , 0.15 , 0.20 } \{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20\} , giving 20 20 threshold combinations. Across this grid, the relationship between trajectory type and optimization outcome is similar across the tested settings. Recovery trajectories have higher success rates than early-stuck trajectories, with odds ratios ranging from 7.35 7.35 to 15.71 15.71 and relative risks from 5.25 5.25 to 10.69 10.69 . Recovery success rates range from 31.4 % 31.4\% to 37.7 % 37.7\% , compared with 3.1 % 3.1\% to 6.8 % 6.8\% for the early-stuck group. Changing the thresholds therefore changes the number of models assigned to each archetype, but the separation between recovery and persistent low-rank trajectories remains present across the tested boundaries.
